skill.hx.pneumonia.risk.title: Risk factors and severity clues
skill.hx.pneumonia.risk.oneLine: What made this patient get pneumonia, and what makes it dangerous
skill.hx.pneumonia.risk.why: The same syndrome in a fit 30-year-old and a frail 80-year-old with diabetes is a different disease in terms of the likely organism, the risk of deterioration, and the required level of care. These questions change the management plan, not just the differential.

asks.text: Age, and whether the patient is normally independent or frail.
Any chronic illness: diabetes, chronic kidney or liver disease, heart failure, COPD or other chronic lung disease.
Anything that suppresses immunity: HIV status if known, chemotherapy, long-term steroids, other immunosuppressants.
Alcohol use, in grams per day or units per week, because of the combined aspiration and pneumococcal risk.
Any problem with swallowing, a recent stroke, or reduced consciousness, which raises the possibility of aspiration.
Recent influenza-like illness, which predisposes to secondary bacterial pneumonia, classically with Staphylococcus aureus.
Vaccination history: pneumococcal and influenza vaccination.
Living situation: a hostel, barracks, care home or other crowded institutional setting.

skill.hx.pneumonia.risk.practice: Take this history from a partner playing an 80-year-old care-home resident with diabetes, and list the risk factors you found in order of how much each one worries you.
pitfalls: Skipping the swallowing and aspiration questions because the patient looks alert at rest.
Not asking about recent influenza, which is a recognised setup for a severe secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Treating vaccination history as an afterthought rather than a modifiable risk factor worth acting on at discharge.
Forgetting that alcohol raises risk through two separate mechanisms, aspiration and impaired host defence, not one.

probes.q: Name three factors that raise the risk of aspiration pneumonia.
probes.a: Reduced consciousness, a recent stroke, and a known swallowing problem. Alcohol intoxication is another.

probes.q: Why ask specifically about a recent influenza-like illness?
probes.a: Influenza predisposes to secondary bacterial pneumonia, classically with Staphylococcus aureus, which can be more severe and cavitating.

probes.q: An 82-year-old care-home resident with pneumonia looks comfortable and is not obviously confused. Should you still worry about severity?
probes.a: Yes. Elderly patients frequently under-present severity: fever may be blunted or absent, tachypnoea may be the only clue, and confusion is best judged against the patient's own baseline by asking a carer or relative, not by your own impression at the bedside.

rubric.text: Asks about relevant comorbidity and immunosuppression
Actively screens for aspiration risk
Asks about pneumococcal and influenza vaccination

teach.heading: Severity is decided at the bedside, before any imaging
teach.body: The decision that matters in pneumonia is not the organism but the disposition: home, ward, or critical care. CURB-65 uses confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age over 65, and every component except urea comes from the history and examination.

rows: Systolic under 90, or diastolic 60 or less

teach.note: Count the respiratory rate yourself for a full minute. It is the most frequently fabricated observation in the chart and one of the most predictive.

teach.heading: Where it was acquired changes the likely organism

points.d: Pneumococcus most often, then atypicals.
Gram negatives and resistant organisms, so the empirical choice differs.
Stroke, reduced consciousness, alcohol, dysphagia. Ask about choking on swallowing.
Steroids, chemotherapy, diabetes, HIV. It widens the differential well beyond the usual organisms.

teach.heading: The features that suggest it is not simple pneumonia
teach.body: Ask about weight loss, night sweats and a cough lasting more than two weeks, because tuberculosis presents as a pneumonia that fails to resolve. Ask about a recent long journey or immobility, because pulmonary embolism with infarction mimics it. Failure to improve after 48 to 72 hours of appropriate treatment should send you back to the history rather than up the antibiotic ladder.

skill.hx.asthma.triggers.title: Triggers, pattern and atopy
skill.hx.asthma.triggers.oneLine: What sets it off, when it happens, and what runs in the family
skill.hx.asthma.triggers.why: A trigger history does two jobs: it supports the diagnosis by showing a pattern that a fixed structural disease cannot produce, and it gives the patient something they can actually act on, which fixed-obstruction disease often cannot offer.

asks.text: What brings an attack on? Ask specifically about exercise, cold air, viral colds, pollen or seasonal change, dust, animal fur or feathers, strong smells, and emotional stress.
Is there a pattern across the day, worse at night or first thing in the morning?
Is there a pattern across the year, worse in a particular season?
Any personal history of eczema, allergic rhinitis (a runny, itchy, blocked nose) or food allergy?
Any family history of asthma, eczema or allergic rhinitis?
Does exercise itself bring on symptoms, and if so, how soon after starting?
Any occupational exposure: flour and grain dust, isocyanates in spray paint, latex, solvents, or animal handling, and whether symptoms are better on days away from work or on holiday?
Has taking aspirin, another NSAID, or a beta blocker, including as eye drops, ever brought on symptoms?

skill.hx.asthma.triggers.practice: Take a trigger history from a partner and, at the end, state out loud whether the pattern you found supports a variable, trigger-related disease or a fixed one.
pitfalls: Asking only about allergens and missing exercise, cold air and viral infection as equally important triggers.
Not asking whether symptoms improve away from work, which is how occupational asthma gets missed.
Forgetting to ask about aspirin, NSAIDs and beta blockers, which can precipitate severe bronchospasm in a susceptible patient.
Treating the family history question as a formality rather than genuinely useful diagnostic information.

probes.q: Name three common triggers for an asthma attack.
probes.a: Exercise, cold air, viral respiratory infection, allergens (pollen, dust, animal fur), strong smells, or emotional stress.

probes.q: A factory worker's wheeze is worse on work days and better on holiday. What does that suggest, and what should you ask next?
probes.a: Occupational asthma. Ask exactly what the work involves and what they are exposed to, such as flour, isocyanates, or latex, and whether colleagues have similar symptoms.

probes.q: Why ask specifically about aspirin, other NSAIDs and beta blockers, including eye drops?
probes.a: They can precipitate severe, sometimes life-threatening bronchospasm in a susceptible asthmatic, including through routes patients may not think to mention, such as an eye drop containing a beta blocker.

rubric.text: Elicits at least three distinct trigger categories
Establishes diurnal or seasonal pattern
Asks about personal and family atopy
Asks about aspirin, NSAIDs and beta blockers

sources.source: GINA Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention

teach.heading: Variability is the diagnosis
teach.body: Asthma is defined by airflow obstruction that varies, so the history is looking for change rather than severity. Diurnal variation, seasonal variation, and symptoms that appear on exposure and settle on removal are what separate it from COPD, which is comparatively fixed and progressive.
teach.note: Waking at night with cough or wheeze is both a diagnostic clue and a control marker, so ask about it at every visit.

teach.heading: Triggers, asked by category

points.d: Dust, pets, pollen, cockroach. Ask what the bedding and the room are like.
Smoke, incense, cooking fumes, perfumes, cold air.
Cough or wheeze minutes into exertion, settling with rest.
Aspirin, NSAIDs, beta blockers including eye drops.
Better at weekends and on holiday is the classic pattern of occupational asthma, and it is only found by asking.

teach.heading: Grading control without a spirometer
teach.body: Four questions grade control anywhere: daytime symptoms more than twice a week, any night waking, reliever use more than twice a week, and any limitation of activity. Any one of them present means the disease is not controlled, regardless of how well the patient says they are managing.

skill.hx.tb.exposure.title: Contact and exposure history
skill.hx.tb.exposure.oneLine: Who this patient has been near, and what has made them vulnerable
skill.hx.tb.exposure.why: TB is a disease that moves through households and communities, and the contact history is not a formality, it is how the next case gets found before they present with advanced disease. It also identifies the host factors that decide whether an exposure became an infection, and whether an infection became active disease.

asks.text: Has anyone in your household, or anyone you spend a lot of time with, ever had a chronic cough, or been diagnosed with or treated for TB?
How many people live in your house, and how many rooms does it have? Ask this even if the answer to the first question is no.
Have you yourself ever been treated for TB before? If so, when, for how long, and did you complete the full course?
Do you know your HIV status? Have you ever been tested?
Do you have diabetes, or are you on any long-term steroid or other treatment that weakens the immune system?
What is your occupation, and specifically, do you work with stone, sand, or in mining, which carries silica exposure?
How have your appetite and weight been over the same period as the cough?
Do you drink alcohol, and roughly how much?

skill.hx.tb.exposure.practice: Take this history from a partner playing a patient who lives in a two-room house with six family members, and identify every modifiable and non-modifiable risk factor you found.
pitfalls: Asking only about contact with a diagnosed TB patient, and not about a chronic cough in the household, which may represent an undiagnosed source case.
Skipping the previous-treatment question, which is essential: incomplete past treatment raises the possibility of drug-resistant disease this time.
Treating the HIV question as optional or awkward rather than a routine, essential part of the assessment.
Not asking about household crowding, which independently predicts transmission risk regardless of a named contact.

probes.q: Name three questions that belong in a TB contact and exposure history.
probes.a: Contact with a chronic cough or known TB case, previous TB treatment and whether it was completed, HIV status, household crowding, diabetes, occupational silica exposure.

probes.q: Why does it matter whether a patient completed a previous course of TB treatment?
probes.a: An incomplete previous course raises the risk of drug-resistant disease, which changes the investigation and treatment approach for the current episode.

probes.q: A patient denies any known TB contact. Should that reassure you?
probes.a: Not fully. Transmission is often from a brief, unrecognised or asymptomatic-seeming contact, and household crowding alone raises risk independent of a named contact. A negative answer narrows but does not exclude the possibility.

rubric.text: Asks about household or close contact with a chronic cough or known TB
Asks about prior TB treatment and completion
Asks about HIV status
Asks about diabetes, immunosuppression and occupational exposure

teach.heading: The exposure history is an epidemiological question, asked kindly
teach.body: Transmission needs a source, proximity and time. Ask who in the house or workplace has had a prolonged cough or has been treated for tuberculosis, how many people share the sleeping room, and how well it is ventilated. Household contact of a sputum positive case is the single highest yield question in the whole history.

points.d: Household, workplace, and anyone treated for TB in the last two years.
How many sleep in the room, and whether there is a window that opens.
Any previous anti-tuberculous treatment, whether it was completed, and for how long. This drives resistance risk.

teach.note: Incomplete or interrupted prior treatment is the strongest historical pointer to drug resistance, and it changes the regimen entirely.

teach.heading: Susceptibility, not just exposure

rows: The strongest single risk for progression to active disease
Both a risk factor and a consequence

teach.heading: The constitutional symptoms are the reason to ask at all
teach.body: Cough for more than two weeks, evening rise of temperature, drenching night sweats, loss of appetite and loss of weight together make tuberculosis likely enough to test, even when the chest sounds normal. Quantify the weight loss and the duration of cough, because those two numbers are what justify sending sputum.

skill.hx.resp.haemoptysis.title: Haemoptysis
skill.hx.resp.haemoptysis.oneLine: Confirm it came from the chest, quantify it, then work out why
skill.hx.resp.haemoptysis.why: Haemoptysis frightens patients and is often under-quantified by clinicians. Two things must happen before any differential: prove the blood is from the airway and not the gut or nose, and measure how much there is, because volume alone can make it an emergency.

asks.text: Did you cough it up, or vomit it, or was it dripping from the back of the nose?
Was it bright red and frothy, or dark like coffee grounds?
How much: streaks in the sputum, a teaspoon, a cup? Ask them to show you with a vessel.
How many times, and over how many days?
What colour is the rest of the sputum, and how much do you bring up in a day?
Any fever, night sweats, weight loss, or cough for more than two weeks?
Any chest pain that catches when you breathe in, or swelling in one calf?
Do you smoke, and for how many pack-years?
Any blood thinners, or any bleeding elsewhere: gums, nose, urine?

teach.heading: First prove it is haemoptysis
teach.note: Also examine the nose and throat. Blood tracking back from a posterior nosebleed is coughed up and mistaken for haemoptysis surprisingly often.

teach.heading: Quantify it, because volume changes the plan
teach.body: Streaking of sputum is not the same problem as frank blood. Massive haemoptysis is a threat to the airway rather than to the haemoglobin: patients drown before they exsanguinate, which is why volume and rate are the urgent measurements and why the bleeding side matters for positioning.

points.d: Usually infection or bronchitis, but still needs a cause in a smoker.
Bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, malignancy, pulmonary embolism.
An emergency. Protect the airway and lie the patient with the bleeding side DOWN to keep blood out of the good lung.

teach.heading: The pattern around the blood names the cause

rows: Cough over two weeks, evening fever, night sweats, weight loss
Large volumes of purulent sputum daily, for years
Smoker, over 40, weight loss, new or changed cough
Sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness, calf swelling
Rusty sputum with acute fever and pleuritic pain
Pulmonary oedema, not a primary lung bleed

pitfalls: Not establishing whether the blood was coughed or vomited before building a differential.
Recording haemoptysis without a volume, so nobody knows if it is streaking or frank blood.
Forgetting the nose and throat as a source.
Missing tuberculosis by not asking about duration of cough, evening fever and weight loss.
Not asking about anticoagulants and bleeding elsewhere.

probes.q: Name two features that separate haemoptysis from haematemesis.
probes.a: Haemoptysis is coughed, bright red, frothy, mixed with sputum and alkaline. Haematemesis is vomited, darker, may contain food, and is acidic.

probes.q: In massive haemoptysis, which side should be dependent, and why?
probes.a: The bleeding side down. The immediate danger is asphyxiation from blood flooding the airways, so gravity is used to keep blood out of the unaffected lung.

probes.q: A 60 year old smoker has haemoptysis, weight loss and a cough that changed character two months ago. Which two diagnoses lead, and which single question best separates them?
probes.a: Bronchogenic carcinoma and pulmonary tuberculosis, which overlap heavily in this presentation. Ask about evening rise of temperature, drenching night sweats and contact with a case of tuberculosis, which point to TB; a changed cough with weight loss in a heavy smoker points to malignancy. Both may need investigating together.

rubric.text: Establishes that the blood was coughed, not vomited or from the nose
Quantifies volume, frequency and duration
Asks about the sputum, fever, weight loss and duration of cough
Covers smoking, anticoagulants and thromboembolic risk

skill.hx.resp.chestpain.title: Pleuritic chest pain
skill.hx.resp.chestpain.oneLine: Does it change with breathing? That one question moves the pain out of the heart and into the chest wall or pleura
skill.hx.resp.chestpain.why: Chest pain that varies with respiration is behaving like pleura or chest wall, not like myocardium. Establishing that early stops a respiratory presentation being worked up as an infarct, and stops a pulmonary embolism being dismissed as muscular.

asks.text: Does the pain change when you breathe in deeply, or when you cough?
Can you point to it with one finger, or is it spread across?
Is it worse in any particular position, or lying on one side?
Did it come on suddenly, over seconds, or build up over days?
Any breathlessness that started at the same time?
Any fever, cough or coloured sputum before the pain?
Any calf pain or swelling, long journey, surgery or period of immobility?
Any rash appearing in a band, or tenderness when I press here?

teach.heading: Respirophasic means pleura or chest wall
teach.body: The parietal pleura is pain sensitive and moves with every breath; the visceral pleura and the myocardium are not. So pain that sharpens on inspiration or coughing is arising from parietal pleura or the chest wall, which reframes the whole differential.

rows: Sudden, with breathlessness, in a tall thin young man
Sudden, with breathlessness and risk factors
Reproduced exactly by pressing on the spot
Band of pain, then vesicles days later
Herpes zoster, painful before the rash
Central, heavy, unaffected by breathing, exertional

teach.note: Pain that you can reproduce exactly by palpating one spot is usually chest wall, but a pulmonary embolism can be tender too. Tenderness reassures only when the risk assessment is otherwise low.

teach.heading: Pleuritic pain that STOPS is not necessarily better
teach.body: As a pleural effusion accumulates, the inflamed pleural surfaces are separated by fluid and stop rubbing, so the pain eases while the breathlessness worsens. A patient reporting that the pain has gone but breathing is harder has usually not improved.

teach.heading: The one that must not be missed
teach.body: Pulmonary embolism presents as sudden pleuritic pain with breathlessness and often nothing to find on examination. Ask every time about calf swelling, recent immobility, long travel, surgery, malignancy, pregnancy and the oral contraceptive pill. The history is where the risk is established, not the chest examination.

pitfalls: Not asking whether the pain varies with respiration, which is the single discriminating question.
Treating reproducible tenderness as proof of a musculoskeletal cause in a patient at risk of embolism.
Reading the resolution of pleuritic pain as improvement when an effusion is forming.
Missing zoster, which is painful for days before the rash appears.

probes.q: Which single question separates pleuritic from cardiac chest pain?
probes.a: Does the pain change with breathing or coughing. Respirophasic pain points to parietal pleura or chest wall, not myocardium.

probes.q: Why does pleuritic pain often ease as a pleural effusion grows?
probes.a: The fluid separates the inflamed parietal and visceral pleural surfaces so they no longer rub, removing the pain while the effusion continues to compromise ventilation.

probes.q: A young man develops sudden right-sided pleuritic pain and breathlessness. Give two diagnoses and the feature of the history that separates them.
probes.a: Spontaneous pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism. Both begin abruptly. The embolism carries thrombotic risk factors, immobility, travel, surgery, malignancy or calf symptoms, while the pneumothorax typically occurs in a tall thin young man at rest with no such risk factors.

rubric.text: Establishes whether the pain varies with respiration
Establishes speed of onset and associated breathlessness
Takes a thromboembolic risk history
Examines for reproducible tenderness and looks for zoster

skill.hx.resp.wheeze.title: Wheeze
skill.hx.resp.wheeze.oneLine: Episodic or continuous, and whether it is really coming from the chest at all
skill.hx.resp.wheeze.why: Wheeze is a musical sound from narrowed intrathoracic airways, and patients apply the word to almost any noisy breathing. Establishing that it is truly a wheeze, and whether it comes and goes, does most of the diagnostic work before a stethoscope is used.

asks.text: Make the sound for me, or describe it. Is it a musical whistle, or noisy breathing?
Is it there all the time, or does it come and go with clear periods between?
Is it worse at night or early morning?
Is it worse breathing in, or breathing out?
What brings it on: dust, smoke, cold air, exercise, a particular room or season?
Any eczema, allergic rhinitis, or family history of asthma or allergy?
Is it better on days away from work, or on holiday?
Did it start suddenly, and could anything have been inhaled?

teach.heading: Episodic or continuous is the first fork

rows: Obstruction of one airway: tumour, foreign body
Sudden onset in a child or a confused adult

teach.note: A wheeze that is always in the same place and never moves is a localised obstruction, not asthma, however wheezy it sounds.

teach.heading: Inspiratory noise is a different emergency
teach.body: Wheeze is predominantly expiratory, because intrathoracic airways narrow further on expiration. A noise that is loudest on INSPIRATION is stridor, arising from the larynx or trachea, and it signals large airway obstruction. Confusing the two delays an airway emergency, so ask which phase is noisier and listen over the neck as well as the chest.
teach.note: Stridor is a reason to call for help now. Wheeze rarely is.

teach.heading: Atopy and the occupational question

points.d: Eczema and allergic rhinitis raise the likelihood of asthma considerably.
Asthma, eczema or hay fever in first degree relatives.
Improvement at weekends and on holiday is the signature of occupational asthma, and it is only ever found by asking.
Beta blockers, including eye drops, and aspirin or other NSAIDs can provoke it.

pitfalls: Accepting the patient's word 'wheeze' without establishing it is a musical, expiratory sound.
Missing stridor by not asking which phase of breathing is noisier.
Calling a fixed unilateral wheeze asthma.
Never asking whether it improves away from work, so occupational asthma is missed.

probes.q: Wheeze is loudest in which phase of respiration, and why?
probes.a: Expiration. Intrathoracic airways narrow further as pleural pressure rises during expiration, so a narrowed airway becomes more obstructed.

probes.q: A noise loudest on inspiration, heard over the neck. What is it, and why does it matter more?
probes.a: Stridor, from obstruction of the larynx or trachea. Extrathoracic airways collapse inward on inspiration. It signals large airway obstruction and is an airway emergency rather than a bronchospasm to be nebulised.

probes.q: A wheeze always heard in the same place, never varying, in a 60 year old smoker. Why is asthma the wrong answer?
probes.a: Asthma is diffuse and variable because bronchospasm affects airways throughout both lungs and changes over time. A fixed, localised, monophonic wheeze indicates narrowing of one airway, so a bronchial carcinoma or an inhaled foreign body must be excluded.

rubric.text: Confirms the sound is a musical expiratory wheeze
Establishes episodic versus continuous, and diurnal variation
Excludes stridor by asking about the inspiratory phase
Covers atopy, family history, occupation and drugs

sources.source: GINA Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention

skill.annex.tobacco.title: Tobacco: pack-years, smoking index and complications
skill.annex.tobacco.oneLine: Two different numbers, two different uses, and they are not interchangeable
skill.annex.tobacco.why: Pack-years and the smoking index both quantify tobacco exposure, but they are calculated differently and used for different things. Confusing them overstates or understates exposure twentyfold.

asks.text: How many cigarettes a day, and for how many years? Include bidis and hookah.
If you have stopped, when did you stop, and what were you smoking before?
Does anyone smoke indoors at home?
What fuel is used for cooking, and is the kitchen ventilated?
Do you chew tobacco, gutkha or paan?
Do you use an electronic cigarette or vape?

teach.heading: Two numbers, and when to use each

rows: packs per day x years (1 pack = 20 cigarettes)

teach.note: Twenty cigarettes a day for 30 years is 30 pack-years and a smoking index of 600. Same patient, same exposure, two very different numbers. Never quote one as the other.

teach.heading: Grading by smoking index

points.d: Mild smoker.
Moderate smoker.
Heavy smoker. Lung cancer is common above this level.

teach.note: For screening, the threshold that matters is pack-years: low-dose CT is considered from age 55 with 30 or more pack-years.

teach.heading: Complications, by system

rows: COPD, cancer of lung, bronchus and trachea, tuberculosis and other respiratory infection, interstitial lung disease, pneumothorax, post-operative complications
Premature coronary disease, peripheral vascular disease and erectile dysfunction, cerebrovascular disease, aortic aneurysm
Gastro-oesophageal reflux, peptic ulceration, pancreatitis, Crohn disease, gallstones in women
Spontaneous abortion, abruptio placentae, premature rupture of membranes, fetal and neonatal death, sudden infant death, postpartum thromboembolism
Dementia and cognitive decline, macular degeneration, cataract
Chronic kidney disease, diabetes, osteoporosis and hip fracture, and increased risk of many infections

teach.note: Three causes account for most smoking-related mortality: atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, lung cancer, and COPD.

teach.heading: The exposures that are not cigarettes
teach.body: Bidis, hookah, chewed tobacco, gutkha and paan all carry risk and are routinely denied when the question is 'do you smoke'. Biomass cooking fuel produces COPD in people who have never smoked, and it is the dominant cause in many Indian women. Second-hand smoke at home counts too. Ask each by name.

teach.heading: Smoking changes how drugs behave
teach.body: Tobacco smoke induces hepatic microsomal enzymes, so the metabolism of several drugs increases and doses that were correct while smoking may become excessive after stopping. Propranolol and theophylline are the classic examples. Reassess doses at cessation rather than months later.

pitfalls: Quoting a smoking index as pack-years, or the reverse.
Asking only about cigarettes, so bidis, hookah and chewed tobacco are missed.
Recording 'ex-smoker' with no quantity and no stop date.
Forgetting biomass fuel exposure in a never-smoker with COPD.
Not reviewing drug doses after cessation, when enzyme induction reverses.

probes.q: Twenty cigarettes a day for 30 years. Give both the pack-years and the smoking index.
probes.a: Thirty pack-years, and a smoking index of 600. Pack-years divides by twenty; the smoking index does not.

probes.q: A never-smoker woman presents with COPD. What exposure must you ask about?
probes.a: Biomass cooking fuel: wood, dung cake, crop residue or coal burned in an unventilated kitchen, often for decades. It is a leading cause of COPD in Indian women.

probes.q: Why might a patient stabilised on theophylline become toxic after they stop smoking?
probes.a: Tobacco smoke induces hepatic microsomal enzymes and accelerates theophylline metabolism. When smoking stops the induction reverses, clearance falls, and an unchanged dose produces rising levels and toxicity.

rubric.text: Obtains cigarettes per day and years, and computes both measures correctly
Asks about bidis, hookah, chewed tobacco and vaping
Asks about cooking fuel and second-hand smoke
Considers enzyme induction and dose review at cessation

skill.annex.defs.resp.title: Definitions: breathlessness and its positional variants
skill.annex.defs.resp.oneLine: Six words that all mean breathless, and the posture that separates them
skill.annex.defs.resp.why: Orthopnoea, platypnoea, trepopnoea and bendopnoea are not synonyms and not interchangeable. Each names a specific relationship between posture and breathlessness, and each points somewhere different, so using the wrong word records the wrong sign.

teach.heading: Posture is the discriminator

rows: Any time. A subjective awareness of uncomfortable breathing
Lying flat, relieved by sitting up
Raised left atrial pressure, heart failure
Waking from sleep, typically 1 to 3 hours after retiring
Sitting or standing UP, relieved by lying down
Right to left shunt, hepatopulmonary syndrome
Bending forward, as when putting on shoes
Raised filling pressures in heart failure

teach.note: Platypnoea is the mirror image of orthopnoea. If you remember only one, remember that: upright makes it worse, lying down relieves it.

teach.heading: Orthodeoxia is a measurement, not a symptom
teach.body: Orthodeoxia is arterial desaturation on standing up. It is what the oximeter shows while the patient describes platypnoea, and the two typically occur together. The mechanism is a right to left shunt that worsens when gravity redistributes blood towards dependent, shunting lung bases, classically in hepatopulmonary syndrome.

teach.heading: Why trepopnoea localises
teach.body: Lying on one side makes that lung dependent, so it receives more perfusion. If that lung is the diseased one, perfusing it worsens ventilation and perfusion mismatch and the patient becomes more hypoxaemic. Patients therefore lie with the GOOD lung down in most unilateral disease, and the side they choose is a clinical sign worth recording.

teach.heading: Two more that are often mixed up

points.d: Defined by volume and rate, not by appearance. The danger is asphyxiation rather than exsanguination, which is why airway protection and positioning come before transfusion.

A forced expiratory manoeuvre against an initially closed glottis. Classified by duration: acute under 3 weeks, subacute 3 to 8 weeks, chronic beyond 8 weeks. The duration bands, not the character, drive the differential.

pitfalls: Writing orthopnoea when the patient means platypnoea, which reverses the implication entirely.
Recording breathlessness without asking which posture changes it.
Treating orthodeoxia and platypnoea as separate findings rather than the same phenomenon measured two ways.
Not noting which side a patient with unilateral lung disease chooses to lie on.

probes.q: A patient is breathless standing and better lying flat. Which term?
probes.a: Platypnoea. It is the opposite of orthopnoea.

probes.q: Why does a patient with unilateral lung disease prefer to lie with the good lung down?
probes.a: The dependent lung receives more perfusion. With the good lung down, perfusion is matched to the lung that is ventilating properly. Lying on the diseased side perfuses the bad lung and worsens the mismatch and the hypoxaemia, which is trepopnoea.

probes.q: Platypnoea with orthodeoxia in a patient with chronic liver disease. What is the mechanism?
probes.a: Hepatopulmonary syndrome: intrapulmonary vascular dilatations act as a right to left shunt, predominantly at the bases. Standing directs more blood to the bases, so shunting increases, saturation falls and breathlessness worsens, and both resolve on lying down.

rubric.text: Establishes which posture provokes and which relieves
Uses the correct term rather than 'breathless'
Records which side the patient lies on in unilateral disease
